title: Practice: Frequency Counters & Grouping with Maps
summary: Solve common backend problems: word frequency counters, grouping items by category, invert a map, and handling missing keys safely.
prerequisites: The Map Contract: Associative Key-Value Storage
learningObjectives: Implement high-throughput frequency counting and histogram patterns
Model one-to-many multimap relationships using Map<K, List<V>>
Invert bidirectional maps safely handling many-to-one collisions
Solve canonical coding interview challenges: Anagram Grouping and First Unique Character
expectedOutcomes: Fluency in standard FAANG-style map aggregation and grouping interview patterns
Mastery of clean grouping logic using modern Java collection idioms

activities.title: Practical Context: Postal Sorting Center Mail Sorting Slots

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Postal Sorting Center Mail Sorting Slots
analogy.story:
In a regional postal distribution center, thousands of letters pour into the facility in mixed piles. Workers stand in front of a grid of pigeonhole slots labeled by postal ZIP code (the key).

As each letter is picked up, the worker looks at the postal code and drops the letter into the corresponding pigeonhole. If a slot already contains letters, the new letter is simply placed on top of the pile (one-to-many list grouping). At the end of the shift, each postal slot contains a ready-to-ship bundle sorted by destination, achieved in a single linear pass.

This is the exact design of multimap grouping in backend engineering.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Grouping maps partition flat streams of data into categorized buckets in O(N) linear time, replacing expensive nested loops.

activities.title: Data Aggregation Patterns: Frequency Tallying & Multimap Grouping

keyTakeaways: Frequency counting maps an item to its occurrence count: Map<Item, Integer>
Multimaps represent one-to-many relationships: Map<Category, List<Item>>
Anagram grouping uses sorted character arrays or frequency fingerprints as keys
Map inversion swaps keys and values, grouping multiple keys that shared identical values into lists

activities.title: Finding the First Non-Repeating Character in O(N)
activities.description: Trace an optimal two-pass algorithm using LinkedHashMap to locate the first unique character in a stream.

steps.description: Construct a LinkedHashMap to simultaneously tally counts and preserve original character encounter sequence.
Tally character frequencies using counts.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) in a single linear pass.
Iterate over entrySet(). The first entry encountered with count == 1 is mathematically guaranteed to be the first unique character.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of computeIfAbsent over if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, new ArrayList<>())?
options: It eliminates redundant hash table lookups and prevents boilerplate null-checking
questions.explanation: computeIfAbsent performs a single hash bucket lookup, initializes the list lazily only when missing, and returns the list reference directly.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of grouping N words of average length K into anagram categories using sorted character keys?
questions.explanation: Sorting the characters of each word takes O(K log K). Doing this for all N words takes O(N * K log K). Inserting into the hash map takes O(1) on average.

questions.question: How should you model an inverted map when original values contain duplicates?
options: Map<V, List<K>> (grouping all matching keys into a list for each unique value)
questions.explanation: Because values in the original map can duplicate, inverting the map means a single original value may map to multiple original keys, requiring Map<V, List<K>>.

questions.question: Why is LinkedHashMap preferred over standard HashMap for the 'First Non-Repeating Character' problem?
options: Because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, allowing Pass 2 to iterate only unique characters in their arrival sequence rather than rescanning the full string
Because HashMap does not support Character keys
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap retains the chronological arrival order of unique characters, so iterating through its entrySet checks unique keys in original arrival order.

questions.question: How would you optimize the canonical Anagram Grouping problem to achieve strictly O(N * K) time complexity?
questions.answer: Instead of sorting the string's characters with Arrays.sort() (which costs O(K log K)), compute a 26-element character frequency array `int[] count = new int[26]`. For example, 'abb' becomes '#1#2#0...'. Using this character count array string as the hash map key takes linear O(K) time per word, resulting in an optimal O(N * K) overall time complexity.

questions.question: How do you find the Top K Frequent Elements in an array of N integers?
questions.answer: 1) Build a frequency map `Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>()` using `freq.merge(n, 1, Integer::sum)` in O(N) time. 2) Insert entries into a min-heap PriorityQueue of bounded size K ordered by frequency in O(N log K) time. Alternatively, use Bucket Sort where bucket index represents frequency count, achieving strictly O(N) time complexity.

questions.question: What happens if a custom object used as a Map key has a hashCode() that always returns 1?
questions.answer: All keys will collide into bucket index 1. The HashMap will degenerate into a single linked list of O(N) length. In Java 8+, if entries exceed 8 and implement Comparable, it converts into a Red-Black tree of O(log N). If entries do NOT implement Comparable, it remains a linked list, degrading all get() and put() operations to O(N) and defeating the purpose of a hash table.

practiceProblems.title: Find First Unique Character Index
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a string s, find the index of the first non-repeating character. If it does not exist, return -1.
hints: Pass 1: Count character frequencies in a HashMap.
Pass 2: Scan string indices and return index where count == 1.

practiceProblems.title: Group Strings by Word Length
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an array of words, return a Map<Integer, List<String>> grouping words by their length using computeIfAbsent.

practiceProblems.title: Invert a One-to-Many Multimap
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a Map<String, List<String>> mapping Department -> List of Employees, return an inverted Map<String, String> mapping Employee -> Department.
hints: For each employee in list, put emp -> dept in the inverted map.

practiceProblems.title: Find Majority Element
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an array of size n, return the majority element that appears more than floor(n/2) times using a frequency map.

practiceProblems.title: Aggregate Transaction Totals by Category
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a list of transaction records with category and amount, return a Map<String, Double> summing the total amount spent per category.
